key_points.point_text: Central thesis: Can't Stop is a masterclass in practical game design, where imperfect mathematical balance is acceptable and rules are used to compensate for it.
key_points.evidence_quote: forced moves compensate combination imbalance ... designers should favor playability over perfection
key_points.reasoning: L002 summary states forced moves balance design; L030 notes forced moves compensate; L031 frames playability over perfection, matching the thesis.

key_points.point_text: Game rules: roll four dice, pair them to move markers on columns 2 through 12, need three completed columns to win; column lengths are 3,5,7,9,11,13,11,9,7,5,3.
key_points.evidence_quote: Board columns 2 to 12 vary 3 to 13 steps; complete three to win
key_points.reasoning: Rules captured but exact column lengths (3,5,7,9,11,13,11,9,7,5,3) are not enumerated, only the 3-to-13 range. Dropped numbers make this Partial.

key_points.point_text: Forced-move rule: if a chosen pairing creates any valid move you must take all legal moves from that pairing, even onto unwanted columns; you cannot cherry-pick.
key_points.evidence_quote: Forced-move rule requires taking every legal move from the chosen pairing
key_points.reasoning: L005 states the rule directly; L006 gives the unwanted-move example, preserving meaning.

key_points.point_text: Two-dice baseline: sum 7 is most likely at 16.67%, exactly 6 times more likely than sum 2 at 2.78%.
key_points.evidence_quote: Two-dice baseline: 7 hits 16.67%, six times more likely than 2
key_points.reasoning: 16.67% and the 6x ratio are present, but the 2.78% baseline probability for sum 2 is dropped. Dropped number caps at Partial.

key_points.point_text: With four dice the distribution flattens: P(can make 7) = 64.4% and P(can make 2) = 13.2%, only a 4.88x ratio versus 6x with two dice.
key_points.evidence_quote: Making a 2 ... about 13.2% ... Making a 7 ... about 64.4% ... Probability ratio 4.88
key_points.reasoning: All three figures (13.2%, 64.4%, 4.88) are captured with correct meaning.

key_points.point_text: Expected rolls to complete a column = length / probability; column 2 needs about 22.73 rolls while column 7 needs about 20.18, so 7 is slightly faster despite being 4x longer.
key_points.evidence_quote: Expected rolls cluster near 20; long column 7 completes slightly faster than 2
key_points.reasoning: The qualitative finding is retained, but the exact expected values 22.73 and 20.18 are dropped. Dropped numbers make this Partial.

key_points.point_text: Column combinations matter: {6,7,8} succeeds 92.0% of the time versus 43.8% for {2,3,12}; all 165 three-column combinations were analyzed, with 37 rated excellent (>=85% success) and a median success of 79.6%.
key_points.evidence_quote: {6,7,8} succeeds 92% per roll; {2,3,12} only 43.8% ... 37 combos rate excellent; median succeeds 79.6%
key_points.reasoning: 92%, 43.8%, 37 and 79.6% captured, but the total count of 165 combinations and the >=85% excellent threshold are dropped. Dropped numbers cap at Partial.

key_points.point_text: "Clean" moves are rare: even the best combination {6,7,8} yields only 39.8% clean rolls, and {2,3,12} only 2.3%, so the forced-move rule contaminates good combinations.
key_points.evidence_quote: Only 39.8% of {6,7,8} rolls are clean; {2,3,12} just 2.3%
key_points.reasoning: Both percentages preserved and the contamination link to forced moves is stated in L030/L035.

key_points.point_text: Stopping heuristic: keep rolling if (P_success x Q) > (P_bust x U), where Q is expected markers advanced and U is unsaved progress; example on {6,7,8} says roll (1.32 > 0.4) and on {2,3,12} says stop (1.12 > 0.46).
key_points.evidence_quote: Stopping rule weighs expected gain against bust-weighted unsaved progress ... Roll on {6,7,8} with five steps banked; stop on {2,3,12} with two
key_points.reasoning: The heuristic's conceptual form and the directional decisions survive, but the explicit inequality and the numeric values 1.32/0.4 and 1.12/0.46 are dropped. Partial.

key_points.point_text: Tournament of 38 strategies across 2,500 head-to-head games each (3.6M total games) found FiftyPercentSurvival the champion at 69.84% win rate, and probabilistic strategies dominate the top rankings.
key_points.evidence_quote: 3.6M-game simulations crown probabilistic, consistent strategies over fast ones ... 38 strategy families ... FiftyPercentSurvival wins 69.84%
key_points.reasoning: 38 strategies, 3.6M games and 69.84% all present, but the 2,500 games per head-to-head pairing is dropped. Dropped number makes this Partial.

key_points.point_text: Consistency beats speed: GreedyUntil1Col is fastest (10.5 turns) but only ranks #11 at 58.90% due to high variance and bust rate, while FiftyPercentSurvival at 11.3 turns wins most.
key_points.evidence_quote: GreedyUntil1Col fastest at 10.5 turns but busts 7.5 times per game ... Consistency beats raw speed
key_points.reasoning: The core contrast and 10.5-turn speed are present, but the #11 ranking, 58.90% win rate and FiftyPercentSurvival's 11.3 turns are dropped. Partial.

key_points.point_text: Significant first-player advantage: P1 wins 55.59% of games for a +11.18% edge, larger than chess (~5%) or Go (~7%); GreedyUntil1Col shows extreme bias at +31.24%.
key_points.evidence_quote: First player wins 55.59%, an 11.18% edge exceeding chess and Go
key_points.reasoning: 55.59%, 11.18% and the chess/Go comparison are retained, but the GreedyUntil1Col +31.24% extreme-bias figure is dropped. Partial.

key_points.point_text: Balance analysis: single-column completion times deviate at most +/-13.6% from 20 rolls, an optimal board one step from current reaches +/-3.09%, and a 20-step board reaches +/-2.17%.
key_points.evidence_quote: Single-column completion deviates at most 13.6% from 20 rolls ... Adding one step per middle column would quadruple balance precision
key_points.reasoning: The 13.6% deviation and the one-step improvement idea are present, but the explicit +/-3.09% and +/-2.17% figures are dropped. Partial.

key_points.point_text: Stated caveat: continuation versus switching strategies were not fully analyzed quantitatively and remain an open question for future work.
key_points.evidence_quote: Continuing current columns usually beats switching, but author hedges: switching unanalyzed quantitatively
key_points.reasoning: The caveat and its quantitative-unanalyzed status are preserved.

key_points.point_text: Recommendations: players should use FiftyPercentSurvival and aim for columns 5-9 while avoiding forced activation of 2-3 and 11-12; designers should prioritize playability and use rules to compensate for imbalance, considering handicaps for turn order.
key_points.evidence_quote: Aim for columns 5-9, avoid edge columns ... designers should favor playability over perfection
key_points.reasoning: The 5-9 target, edge avoidance and playability advice are present, but the explicit FiftyPercentSurvival player recommendation and the turn-order handicap suggestion are not captured. Partial.
